I hate the chip in the US at the moment.

Successfully inserting the card is a far clunkier maneuver then successfully swiping it: swipe channels are usually pointed upwards toward your eyes and easy to locate - with a little LED - whereas every single chip terminal I have seen is a horizontal slit that you have to guess at the location of or feel with your hands to position the card correctly.

Then the card has to remain in the device while the transaction happens, which often means the wallet has to remain in hand, which prevents me from doing things with that hand to finish the rest of the transaction.

All this in the name of better security would at least be understandable, except we don't have chip-and-pin in the US: we have chip-and-signature with no validation on the signature whatsoever! This protects against people that have skimmed the card information and attempted to write it on to a different card... But not against misuse of lost or stolen cards. Why? Why did the US choose the halfway approach*?

I always choose to swipe instead of inserting the card if I can get away with it. I avoid shopping at Walmart now that they require chip transactions. Until it expired, I carried my old version of my card without a chip and swiped that everywhere so that even places that required a chip could not force me to use it.

Long story short, in my opinion: merchants aren't adopting it because it's a worse experience for their customers. Europe has this figured out, with chip-and-pin and card readers With vertical slots like a toaster which are easy to get the card into... Never seen that stateside.

This rant wasn't terribly related to the article, but it had been stewing for a while and this gave me an excuse to type it out.

* Speaking of credit cards here. I never use a debit card in stores, so I don't know what it's like to do that with a chip.
